title: General equilibrium theory

definition.text: The branch of economics that studies supply, demand and prices across a whole economy of many linked markets, seeking to show that together they reach an overall equilibrium.

facts.text: It contrasts with partial equilibrium, which studies one part of the economy while holding everything else fixed.
It goes back to Léon Walras's Elements of Pure Economics of 1874 and took its modern form in the 1950s with Arrow, Debreu and McKenzie.
The first welfare theorem says market equilibria are Pareto efficient: no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
The first welfare theorem quietly assumes complete markets and perfect information.

The second welfare theorem says any efficient outcome can be reached by redistributing starting endowments and then leaving the market alone, suggesting efficiency and fairness can be handled separately.
From the 1970s, faster computers and input–output tables let economists solve general equilibrium models of real national and world economies numerically.
Computable general equilibrium models use real economic data to estimate how an economy might respond to changes in policy or technology.
Keynesian and Post-Keynesian economists reject the theory as misleading, arguing that real economies are not in equilibrium.

contested_note: General equilibrium theory is a central dispute between neoclassical economists and other schools, some of which call it misleading and useless.

title: Imperfect competition

definition.text: Any market that falls short of at least one of the conditions of a perfectly competitive market.

facts.text: Imperfect competition makes markets inefficient and so leads to market failure.
A market is imperfect if sellers can set their own prices, there is only one seller, entry is blocked, buyers and sellers know different things, or products differ.
The more a firm can lift price above marginal cost, the greater the inefficiency; at the extreme, a monopoly overcharges and underproduces.
The broad imperfect market structures include monopolistic competition, where many firms sell slightly different products, and oligopoly, where a few firms each sway the others.
A firm in an imperfect market faces a downward-sloping demand curve, unlike the flat demand curve facing a perfectly competitive firm.
Some theorists hold that no real market has ever met the conditions of perfect competition.

contested_note: Economists dispute whether economic policy should assume perfect or imperfect competition.

definition.text: A measure of how concentrated a market is, found by adding up the squares of every firm's market share.

facts.text: It gives big firms more weight than a simple concentration ratio does.
It runs from 1/N to 1, where N is the number of firms; the more concentrated the market, the higher the value.

definition.text: How strongly the quantity of a good people buy responds to a change in their income.

facts.text: It is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income: if a 10% rise in income lifts demand by 20%, it is 2.0.
Normal goods have positive income elasticity and inferior goods negative; below 1 marks a necessity and above 1 a luxury.
Food as a whole has an income elasticity between zero and one, so spending on food grows more slowly than income, an observation called Engel's law.
Estimates for gasoline in developed economies range from 0.66 to 1.26.
Income elasticities for food and energy tend to fall as incomes rise: for cereals, from 0.62 in Tanzania to 0.05 in the United States.
As economies get richer, spending shifts toward services, which need fewer commodities to produce.
Most measures of environmental damage rise with income, though with an income elasticity below one.
